Workstation & editor · 1/5

Commits, branches and HEAD

  1. 1Commit: a snapshot plus a parent link
  2. 2Branch: a pointer to one commit
  3. 3HEAD: the branch you are on
  4. 4New commit: your branch moves forward

Workstation & editor · 2/5

One history forks into two

feature

  • C3, parent C2
  • feature points to C3

main

  • C4, parent C2
  • main points to C4

C2 is the common ancestor of both tips.

Workstation & editor · 3/5

git merge feature, on main

  1. 1Find the common ancestor C2
  2. 2Three-way merge of C4 and C3
  3. 3Record merge commit C5 with two parents
  4. 4main moves to C5, feature stays at C3

Workstation & editor · 4/5

git rebase main, on feature

  1. 1Save the change that C3 made
  2. 2Reset feature to C4, the tip of main
  3. 3Apply the change as new commit C3'
  4. 4History is one straight line

Workstation & editor · 5/5

Same files, different history

Merge

  • Keeps both lines of work
  • Adds a commit with two parents
  • Rewrites no commits

Rebase

  • One straight line
  • Creates new commits
  • Safe for local commits only

Do not rebase commits that exist outside your repository.

Each commit stores a snapshot and a link to its parent.

A branch is a movable pointer, and HEAD names your current branch.

Now the history forks into two lines.

Feature adds C3, main adds C4,

and both commits have the parent C2.

On main, git merge feature combines C4,

C3 and their common ancestor C2.

Git records C5, a merge commit with two parents.

On feature, git rebase main replays the change of C3

on top of C4 as a new commit, C3'.

History becomes a straight line.

Both commands give the same final files, but rebase rewrites commits.

Never rebase commits that exist outside your repository.
